title_original: Todd Boehly: “Europe isn’t competitive because it hasn’t had to defend itself”
excerpt_original: “Why aren’t there trillion-dollar companies in Europe? Because you’re not having to compete every day.”

blocks.text: Todd Boehly, co-founder and chairman of US holding company Eldridge Industries, has delivered a scathing critique of European business practices, saying the continent “has been subsidised for 75 years.”

“Is that the reason [European companies] are not as competitive?” said Boehly, speaking in the Fireside Chat as the closing session of Doha Film Festival’s Doha Industry Days. “If you start to unpack why things are competitive or not, ultimately Europe hasn’t had to defend itself, because that was the deal after the Second World War.
“The reality is, why aren’t there any trillion-dollar companies in Europe? It’s because if you’re not out there having to compete every day, you’re not ferocious at doing what you need to do.”
US businessman Boehly is co-founder and chairman of Eldridge Industries, which invests in insurance, asset management, technology, sports, media, real estate, and the consumer sector.

Eldridge put the initial seed funding into US producer-distributor A24, and remains a minority stakeholder in the company. Eldridge has also put financing into James Corden and Ben Winston’s Fulwell 73, and independent studio MRC, retaining a minority stake in the latter after separating assets in 2022.

During the half-hour conversation, Boehly repeatedly advocated for businesses, including film companies, existing without outside support. “If something is not walking on its own two feet, at some point it won’t survive,” said Boehly. “Someone gets tired of cutting cheques. Once it becomes a crutch, it becomes no good.”

The executive also touched on key industry topics including major mergers such as that of Paramount and Warner Bros. Boehly said he did not believe it would dampen the prospects of smaller, independent firms. “I think that’s wrong,” said Boehly. “Humans are extremely capable; when you find capable humans that have a differentiated view, you’re going to be able to continue to work outside. It’s rare you have something like an A24. You’re going to continue to see opportunity. Backrooms shows you there’s a lot of room for this young talent.”
He spoke glowingly about A24 founder Daniel Katz, who, pre-founding A24, led the film finance group at investment firm Guggenheim Partners, of which Boehly was president.

“There are very few entertainment people who understand math,” said Boehly. “It’s about how are you taking and distributing risk. What Daniel was really good at, becaue he sat on a trading desk – he understood how to get his money back using different windows.”

Boehly also backed the theatrical experience, mentioning its rebound this year on several occasions. “There’s a natural inclination to filmmakers to want to have that experience and not go right to streaming,” said the executive. “It’s an economic proposition that might make sense, but it isn’t what the essence of the industry is.”

Across the session, Boehly offered a blunt outlook of business practices within the film world. “You have to be in business,” he said. “It’s called showbusiness. It’s not called show fun. If you end up with less money every time you play, you’re going to end up losing. These are not charities.
Away from film, Boehly is the former co-controlling owner and chairman of Premier League football club Chelsea, and former co-owner of Ligue 1 team Strasbourg, under the BlueCo consortium.
Doha Film Festival continues until Friday, November 27.
